faq.a: It indicates bleeding into the skin from DIC, a hallmark of meningococcemia.
faq.q: Why is a non‑blanching rash a red flag?

faq.a: Yes; up to 30 % present with isolated sepsis and rash.
Use high‑dose chloramphenicol (if susceptibility known) or a carbapenem, acknowledging higher toxicity.

exam: A 4‑year‑old presents with fever, vomiting and a non‑blanching rash. What is your immediate management? — ABCs, give ceftriaxone, start fluid bolus, assess for shock.
How does meningococcemia differ from meningitis in presentation? — Rash and shock are prominent in meningococcemia; neck stiffness more common in meningitis.
What laboratory finding confirms DIC in this patient? — Prolonged PT/aPTT, low fibrinogen, thrombocytopenia.
Why is ceftriaxone preferred over penicillin in many East African settings? — Rising penicillin resistance and better CSF penetration.
A patient is allergic to β‑lactams. What alternative antibiotic can be used? — Chloramphenicol (if local susceptibility) or a fluoroquinolone, noting toxicity.

Explain how you would differentiate meningococcemia from severe dengue in a febrile patient with rash. — Dengue rash is blanching, platelets drop later; dengue has positive NS1/IgM, no purpura necrosis.
What are the key steps if the patient develops refractory hypotension despite fluids? — Initiate vasopressor (norepinephrine), monitor urine output, consider adrenal insufficiency.
ai.title: Meningococcemia
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Meningococcemia is a rapidly progressive bloodstream infection caused by Neisseria meningitidis. It presents with fever, rash, shock and can quickly lead to death if not recognised and treated promptly.

b: Incubation 2‑10 days
Peak incidence in children <5 yr and adolescents
High case‑fatality rate (10‑15 %) without treatment
sections.p: Neisseria meningitidis is a gram‑negative diplococcus transmitted by respiratory droplets. Invasive disease can manifest as meningitis, meningococcemia, or both. In low‑resource settings, outbreaks are common in crowded living conditions.

b: Diagnostic criteria: fever, hypotension, purpuric rash, positive blood culture for N. meningitidis
Severity staging: mild (stable vitals), moderate (tachycardia, capillary refill >2 s), severe (shock, DIC, multi‑organ failure)
Common co‑factors in East Africa: HIV, malnutrition, recent viral illness
sections.p: Meningococcemia is diagnosed clinically and confirmed by blood culture or PCR. The classic petechial/purpuric rash reflects disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). Early recognition and empiric antibiotics are lifesaving.

b: Look for neck stiffness, but its absence does not rule out disease
Assess for meningitis signs (photophobia, Kernig’s sign) – treat both if present
Identify shock: cold clammy skin, tachycardia, hypotension
sections.p: Patients often present to district hospitals with fever, headache, vomiting and a rapidly spreading non‑blanching rash. Rapid deterioration can occur within hours, making early empiric therapy essential.

t.a: Lumbar puncture (if no meningitis signs and stable)

b: Avoid penicillin if local resistance >10 %
Fluid resuscitation: isotonic crystalloids 20 ml/kg bolus, repeat as needed
Vasopressors (e.g., norepinephrine) for refractory hypotension
Consider fresh frozen plasma or platelets if DIC severe
sections.p: Start high‑dose intravenous ceftriaxone or cefotaxime immediately; give supportive care for shock and DIC. Give prophylaxis to close contacts.

b: Septicemia from Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pneumoniae
Viral hemorrhagic fevers (e.g., Ebola, dengue) – consider travel history
Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura – labs show normal PT/aPTT
sections.p: Other causes of acute purpuric rash and shock can mimic meningococcemia.

b: Negative culture does not rule out meningococcemia if antibiotics given
Mild thrombocytopenia can be early DIC – repeat labs
sections.p: Early blood cultures may be negative after antibiotics; a normal platelet count does not exclude early DIC.

b: Describe the rash: non‑blanching petechiae → purpura → necrosis
Explain why ceftriaxone is first‑line (broad coverage, good CSF penetration)
State the immediate steps for a patient in shock (ABC, fluids, antibiotics)
Identify prophylaxis strategy for contacts
sections.p: Examiners test your ability to recognise the emergency, order appropriate tests, start therapy, and manage complications.

whenToSeekHelp: Signs of shock (BP < 90 mmHg, capillary refill >2 s)
